turns.question: Why is there a big drop in pH on Sept 26?
turns.answer:
Over Sept 24–28 (the window I pulled, which is complete), the Sept 26 drop was actually the collapse of a spike — pH didn't fall from its usual level, it shot far above it first, then crashed through it and kept going 【T1】:

- **Sept 24–25:** pH steady around 7.40–7.50.
- **Late Sept 25 into Sept 26 (UTC):** a sudden jump from 8.12 to 11.83 between 01:26 and 01:56 UTC (~18:00 local on Sept 25), then a climb to about 12.9, where it sat for roughly 14 hours.
- **Sept 26 daytime:** the crash you're seeing — a sudden fall from 11.21 to 6.36 at 17:56 UTC (~10:00 local), then ~7.0–7.2 by evening.
- **Sept 27–28:** it kept falling — ~5 on Sept 27, bottoming at 3.418, and still only ~3.4–4.3 through the end of Sept 28.

Against the operator's configured pH thresholds of 6–10, the pod flagged pH **high** Sept 26 11:26–17:26 UTC (highest 11.92) and **low** Sept 27 01:56 UTC to Sept 28 23:30 UTC (lowest 3.418) 【T1】. It also marked 30 readings in this window as very unusual, including 12.19–12.48 and 2.3–2.73 described as outside the range natural water spans, plus several sudden jumps 【T1】.

**What the other channels did at the same time 【T2】:**
- Conductivity rose in step with the high pH — from ~59,000–61,000 µS/cm up to ~70,900 — then fell back to ~58,400 as pH collapsed.
- Temperature fell from ~84 °F to ~68 °F over the same hours, then recovered.
- DO stayed steady (~7.9–10.7 mg/L) and ORP moved only slightly (~224→238 mV).

**On the why:** the sensor data can't establish a cause. The loaded guidance does list one event signature with this shape — industrial or chemical discharge, "Abrupt step changes in conductivity, pH, or ORP with no diel, tidal, or rainfall explanation" 【10】 — with the discriminator that "A real discharge usually affects more than one parameter in a chemically consistent way and changes gradually as a plume arrives. A fault often affects one channel, or all channels at the identical timestamp." 【10】. The pH-and-conductivity step here is consistent with that signature, but I can't confirm what happened from this data; a calibration check would confirm the readings, and a site visit would help settle it.

Two caveats: the pod looks to have been serviced or out of the water Sept 24 22:45–Sept 25 00:25 UTC (those 5 readings are excluded), just before this event, and the turbidity sensor appears to have failed (readings stuck at one value all window, left out of every metric — it should be inspected), so turbidity can't help cross-check this. The pod last reported Oct 13, 16 days ago.

turns.question: Why is there a big drop in pH on Sept 26?
turns.answer:
## What actually happened around Sept 26

The drop was the second half of a larger episode — pH first spiked *up*, then collapsed. Through Sept 25 pH sat near 7.4–7.5, then (times in UTC, pod "Algalita Pod", Los Alamitos Bay):

- **The rise:** 8.12 at 01:26 on Sept 26 → 11.83 at 01:56 → 12.19 → 12.45, readings the device flagged as "outside the range natural water spans" 【T1】. It peaked at 12.91 and held ~11.6–12.5 for hours, sitting above the pod's configured 6–10 alert limits from 11:26 to 17:26 UTC (highest 11.92) 【T1】.
- **The drop:** it fell to 6.36 at 17:56 UTC (from 11.21) — about 10 am local solar time on Sept 26 — hovered near 7, then crashed to 2.73 at 00:56 UTC on Sept 27, about 5 pm local on Sept 26 【T1】. The device flagged the whole stretch, Sept 26 02:26 – Sept 27 00:56 UTC, as unusual (2.73 to 12.91) 【T1】.
- **Aftermath:** pH stayed below the configured limits from 01:56 UTC Sept 27 to 23:30 UTC Sept 29 (lowest 3.418), recovering only to ~5.7 by the end of that window. Both flags have since cleared 【T1】.

## What the other sensors did at the same time

- **Conductivity** jumped from ~59,000 to ~71,000 µS/cm and back within the same ~18 hours 【T1】.
- **Temperature** fell from ~84 °F to ~67 °F, then rose to ~85 °F 【T1】.
- **ORP** rose from ~224 to ~238 mV, then eased back; **DO** dipped from ~9.7 to ~7.9 mg/L with two flagged spike readings 【T1】.
- **Turbidity can't help diagnose this** — its readings were stuck over Sept 23–Oct 3 and were excluded as a likely failed sensor; the tool note says that sensor should be inspected 【T1】. (A separate servicing-style stretch, Sept 24 22:45–Sept 25 00:25 UTC, was also excluded from every metric.)

## Why — what the data can and can't say

These readings show *what* happened, not *why* — nothing here measures tides, weather, rain, or nearby activity, so I can't name a cause. The loaded guidance says to check "Sensor Fault Signatures (Check First)" 【10†"Sensor Fault Signatures (Check First)"】 and gives this discriminator: "A real discharge usually affects more than one parameter in a chemically consistent way" and changes gradually as a plume arrives, while "A fault often affects one channel, or all channels at the identical timestamp." 【10†"A fault often affects one channel, or all channels at the identical timestamp."】 The industrial/chemical-discharge signature, for its part, is "Abrupt step changes in conductivity, pH, or ORP with no diel, tidal, or rainfall explanation." 【10†"Abrupt step changes in conductivity, pH, or ORP with no diel, tidal, or rainfall explanation."】 What you see here — several channels moving together, but in abrupt steps rather than a gradual plume arrival, with swings (pH 12.9 → 2.3) far outside anything natural water spans — doesn't settle cleanly on either side. A real event would also need to be "not explained by upwelling, internal tides, heatwave, or direct rainfall" 【1†"not explained by upwelling, internal tides, heatwave, or direct rainfall"】 and show "a correlated shift in two or more parameters consistent with a signature in Section 6" 【1†"Shows a correlated shift in two or more parameters consistent with a signature in Section 6"】.
